speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:-

The Moosejaw Morning News on the 6th instant contained an editorial statement to the effect that this Government will introduce legislation for the purpose of substantially reducing the duty on agricultural implements. I know I would not be in order if I asked the Prime Minister whether the report were true or not, because this is probably not the time to discuss tariff matters; but I would ask the right hon. gentleman whether there is any foundation for the report or whether there has been any utterance by any member of the Government which would be a justification for the report that this Government will introduce legislation substantially to reduce the duties on agricultural implements.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I am constrained to answer the hon. gentleman's question in the way that he suggests another question should be answered.
I just wish to ask what the Prime Minister meant by his answer. Did he mean that there had been no announcement made of the proposed reduction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I meant exactly what I
said to my hon. friend. Announcements with regard to the tariff are made in this House in the first instance, and on the proper occasion.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I am advised by a person resident in the county of Victoria, Nova Scotia, where a provincial election is now being held, that is, the election which was referred to last week in connection with the customs boat Alert, that persons supporting the Conservative candidate in that election are publicly saying that the Supplementary Estimates contain specific votes for expenditures in specific localities in the county of Victoria. I desire to ask the Minister of Public Works if there is any authority for such statements or if any person is authorized to make a statement to that effect and if such statements

have any foundation in fact. The minister will remember the occurence of a similar matter about a year ago in connection with a provincial election in the county of Antigonish, and I think the Minister of Public Works stated' in Parliament that he deprecated such conduct on the part of any person. Has anybody been authorized to make a statement of this kind, and have advance copies of the Supplementary Estimates been issued from his department and information contained in them placed in the possession of any person?

Of course, I am not in any way responsible for any statement that my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax may have heard or any reports he may have seen, and not having information as to the exact report or statement to which he refers it would be impossible for me to give a definite answer as far as that part of my hon. friend's question is concerned. I may say, however, in respect to Supplementary Estimates, that whatever we may have under consideration for works to be carried on in this particular locality, the county of Victoria, I believe, they have not been published nor has any information, so far as I am aware, been given to any individual outside of the department.

Has there been
any definite conclusion about any expenditure ?

With respect to definite
conclusions they will only be announced when the Supplementary Estimates are brought down to the House.

He said: I desire to avail myself of this opportunity of discussing briefly the matter of the contract for the transatlantic mail service, the selection of the winter ports for this mail service, and what I believe to be the unjustifiable interference of the Gov-



eminent in connection with the selection of the winter mail ports.
Some few months ago it became necessary, under a contract made about a year ago with certain steamship companies for the performance of the transatlantic mail service, to select or designate the winter port at which the mails would be received and from which they would depart. This matter was, of course, of very considerable interest to the only two Atlantic ports suitable for the winter mail service, namely Halifax and St. John. The matter was the occasion of a great deal of local interest in these two ports, but I did not wish to accentuate local feeling in the matter. I do not propose discussing this matter purely from the point of the merits of these two respective ports. That can better be done when discussing the next contract. The transatlantic mail service, performed at a cost to this country of $1,000,000 is consequently a matter of interest to Canada generally. The various sections of the country are very much interested in the promptitude with which transatlantic mails are received and distributed throughout Canada. Prom my knowledge of occurrences during the past few months in connection with this matter, I desire to say that there has been an unnecessary and unjustifiable interference on the part of the Government with the transatlantic mail contract, in so far as it affects the winter service, which calls for some explanation.
.1 may point out to the House that prior to last year, when the existing contract was concluded, it was the practice for the contracting steamship companies to embark mails at Halifax on going to British ports, and land mails at that port on returning to Canada. This method has prevailed for a number of years, not to the entire satisfaction, I believe of the steamship companies. Last year, however, a new contract was entered into with certain steamship companies by the Postmaster General on behalf of the Government of Canada, providing for a more frequent mail service, and leaving to the contracting companies the selection of Canadian ports of arrival and, departure for the summer and winter service. For the summer service the contracting steamship companies were to select either Montreal or Quebec, or both; in any event, I think the mails were to be landed at Quebec. For the winter season it was at the option of the contracting companies to adopt either of the ports of Halifax or St. John. When the terms of this contract were presented to the House by the Post-
master General last year, he said, respecting the ports to be selected for the winter service:
The ships can start from whatever port the companies please provided they do not start from any but a Canadian port, namely, Montreal or Quebec in summer, and St. John or Halifax in winter.
Mr. Pugsley: Not both?
Mr. Pelletier:	Halifax or St. John at
the option of the contractors, which means that each of the ports will stand on Its own merits. We undertake to deliver the mails through whichever of the ports the companies will choose, for both the winter and the summer services.
It will be observed that this is a very clear and explicit declaration of policy on the part of the Government that, having regard to the winter mail service, the contracting steamship companies were at liberty to make selection of whichever port they chose. This clearly was 4 p.m. the intention of the Government, and the same idea was reiterated by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) in a speech delivered at St. John some time in November last in which he dealt with this particular matter, which was of very great interest to the people of his city and constituency. On this occasion the Minister of Marine and Fisheries spoke as follows:
The question of the carriage of mails from Canada to Great Britain has been one that has caused for a good many years past a great deal of discussion, and with a view to having more frequent carriage Of mails and a better service upon the Atlantic, the Postmaster General entered last spring into a new arrangement by which eight steamers belonging respectively to the Allan Line, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Steamship Companies, would undertake this work, giving more frequent mail connection between Canada and Great Britain, during both summer and winter. Under contracts which have hitherto prevailed, the mail steamers of the Canadian Pacific Railway and Allan Lines have been compelled to leave their mails at Halifax and then come on to St. John. St. John was in no sense a mail port so far as the contract for the carriage of the mails entered into by the Liberals was concerned. The general demand in St. John was that each port should stand on its own merits, and that it should be optional with the contractors to select whichever port-they chose on the Atlantic for the reception and discharge of the mails that they carried across the ocean. Under the contract for an improved mail service entered into by the Postmaster General in April, last, which is to continue for one year and which called for three sailings each week in summer and two in winter, this provision was inserted, and mails will be delivered to and taken from steamers at Halifax and St. John at the contractors option, and it was generally felt that the result would be to-

fairly test the merits of the two ports so far as mails were concerned.
So, here again, there was a very clear and plain declaration of policy in respect to the selection of ports by the contracting steamship company. According to the statement of the Minister of Marine, the optional feature of the contract was inserted for the purpose of testing the relative merits of St. John and Halifax as winter mail ports, or for the purpose of permitting the contracting steamship companies to be arbiters on this point, thus relieving the Government of this difficult duty. The optional features of the winter mail service contract was also agreeable to the Boards of Trade of the cities of St. John and Halifax, although at first there was, I think, some opposition at Halifax to this suggestion owing, I suppose, to the fact that for a long period transatlantic mails were embarked and landed at the port of Halifax. So far as I was personally concerned, at last session of Parliament when this contract was before us for consideration, I considered on the whole the proposition eminently fair, although a great deal might have been said, for an express stipulation that the port of Halifax be selected as the winter mail port because it afforded the shortest route and its merits for such purpose had been well established. Now, under this feature of the contract, namely the right of selection by the contracting steamship companies, the Canadian Pacific railway steamship line, the Allan steamship line, and the Royal line of steamships, selected Halifax as their port of arrival and departure in connection with the mail service. In addition to that the White Star line which was to substitute in the event of any of the ships hf the contracting steamship companies being out of commission at any time during the life of the contract, had also selected the port of Halifax under the contract, l believe the selection by the contracting steamship companies was made without any political influence whatever. Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy, president of the Canadian Pacific railway, stated publicly in an interview that the selection was made by his company without suggestions on the part of the Government, and that in no respect was the Government a factor in the selection of that port. They intimated that one of the reasons for the selection of the port of Halifax was the lack of sufficient facilities at the port of St. John, besides, they disliked the two-port call as under previous contracts. But, at any rate, I think I am justified in saying that the selection of the port of 37i
Halifax by the Canadian Pacific railway company was made strictly on the merits of that port. This naturally caused a great deal of opposition in the city of St. John. So pronounced was the dissatisfaction against the selection made by the contracting steamship companies that the political friends of the Government were most pronounced in their denunciation of the Government whom they charged with responsibility for permitting the port selection which [DOT]had been made. In the city of St. John there is a political club named after the Prime Minister of the country, and so antagonistic were they to the selection which was made by the Canadian Pacific railway steamships particularly, and the complicity of the Government therein as they imagined, that the officers of that club saw fit to resign from office.

Surely I have not been misinformed. At least a statement to that effect appeared in the newspapers of St. John and Halifax, and I do not remember ever seeing it contradicted; but I suppose the Minister of Marine will admit that a great deal of hostile opinion was expressed by members of that club in connection with this particular matter.
