That is a matter of not very great importance, and 1 think we may continue to disagree about it Public opinion was so hostile in St. John as to the action of the contracting steamship companies that a request, it is also said, was made by some of the political friends of the Minister of Marine that he should resign his seat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not true at all.

I simply made the remark that this was said. A great many things were perhaps said by the newspapers during the heat of the controversy over this matter that were not strictly accurate. It was charged that the Minister of Marine was actively engaged negotiating with the Canadian Pacific railway for the purpose of inducing them, if possible, to make a change in the port which they had designated under the transatlantic mail contract. I suppose the

Minister of Marine will hardly undertake to deny that. However, the point I wish to emphasize here is that the steamship companies, whose names I have already mentioned designated the port of Halifax as the port from which and at which they would perform their transatlantic mail contract. The selection occasioned a great deal of opposition in the city of St. John, and I think there is evidence that the Government or individual members of the Government intervened and sought to nullify the right of selections which had been exercised by the contracting steamship companies for purely political purposes.
As I have already said, it was rumoured that negotiations were conducted with the Canadian Pacific railway by members of *the Government for the purpose, if possible, of inducing them to revert to the port of St. John instead of the port of Halifax. But it would appear that the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company were invulnerable, and declined to recede from the selection which they had previously made of the port of Halifax. It is unfortunately correct, however, that another steamship company, namely the Royal Line, owned by the Canadian Northern railway, which had also designated Halifax as its port under the contract, subsequently receded from that selection and designated St. John; and it is that particular matter which I desire to bring to the attention of the Government. I believe it is absolutely correct, and beyond contradiction, that this change was made owing to pressure brought to bear .upon this company by the Government of Canada, or by some members of the Government. I say, and I say without fear of any successful contradiction, that this change would not have been made except under the greatest pressure possible or imaginable. The Royal Line of steamships had operated from the port of Halifax for three years preceding this. Sir William Mackenzie, the president of the Canadian Northern railway, on many occasions publicly and privately stated that Halifax would continue to be the port of the Royal Line. At the time, rumours began to float about, that in consequence of the selection of the port of Halifax by the Canadian Pacific Steamship Line the Royal Line would be forced to select the port of St. John in order to pacify party interests there, enquiries were made of the officials of the Canadian Northern railway by .the two papers published1 an Halifax-the Morning Chronicle and the Halifax Herald -and also by the Halifax Board of Trade,

as to whether such a change was contemplated by the Canadian Northern railway. To each of these three inquiries, a very prompt, specific, and emphatic answer was given by Mr. Hanna, first vice-president of the Canadian Northern railway, that no such change was contemplated by (that company, that Halifax was the port of the Royal Steamship Line and they proposed to continue it as such. The fact is, however, that shortly after this the Royal Line did officially announce that their two steamships, the Royal George and the Royal Edward, would sail from the port of St. John during .the winter of 1913-14, and would perform its part of the transatlantic mail contract from that port. I have not the slightest hesitancy in saying that the officials of the Royal Steamship Line and the directors of the Canadian Northern railway protested against leaving the port of Halifax and adopting the port of St. John. I make this statement boldly, and emphatically, and challenge any member of the Government to say whether or not I am correct in this regard. Shortly after the adoption of the port of St. John, Sir William Mackenzie landed there from England, and was interviewed by a representative of one of the St. John newspapers. He was naturally .interrogated as to the mail contract and the adoption of the port of St. John by his company, and he is reported to have spoken as follows to the reporter:
With regard to the probable terminus ot our Atlantic steamship line in winter, we have been working from Halifax and were quite satisfied with the route. I am not yet familiar with the reasons which led to the change this winter, and do not know that it will be continued. At any rate^we have not made any plans for sending our steamers to St. John another winter, and it is impossible to say where they will go-
But, Sir William, the rail haul is considerably less from St. John,' said the reporter.
* Well, we have been working with the Intercolonial railway and would be quite satisfied to continue to do so,' was the reply.
Therefore I .say that so far as the official head of the Royal Steamship Line is concerned, it is evidently clear that he at that moment knew little of the reasons which operated to bring about a change in the port of departure for the Royal Line. It is also quite clear that he was perfectly satisfied with the port of Halifax which they had adopted and constantly used for the preceding three years, and I think, Mr. Speaker, this is some evidence, at least, of pressure of some kind or another having been exerted by some person upon this particular steamship company. The St.

John Standard, a newspaper favourable to the Ministry publicly stated that this change made by the Royal Line was at the request of the Government. I am of course unable to say whether there was justification for that statement or not. The Halifax Herald, another journal sympathetic to the Administration, stated that tremendous influences must have been exerted upon the Royal Line in order to induce them to abandon the port of Halifax. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries was evidently very much interested in the state of feelings which prevailed in the city of St.John. That was only natural, and any hon. gentleman I think would naturally sympathize with him in the circumstances, which were most uncomfortable. I think it was just immediately before the adoption of the port of St. John by the Royal Line was made public that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries went to that city, accompanied by the Minister of Public Works, and there publicly made the statement that the Royal Line of Steamships would for the present season use the port of St. John. I think I may fairly say that when the Minister of Marine went to the city of St. John for the purpose of making this announcement, he evidently intended to take to himself the credit for the change made by this particular steamship line, and it is a very fair inference I think for me to make that the change was made through the interference and influence of the Government, and in that change the Minister of Marine played quite a part. I think there is also no doubt whatever but that some members of the Government endeavoured to influence the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to revert to the port of St. John. That company was invulnerable. Failing in this respect, the Government, or members of the Government, I suppose thought they would then attack that steamship company which was the most vulnerable, and naturally they selected the line of steamships operating under the name of the Royal Line, and owned by the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Just here, one might fairly protest against the pressure brought on this particular steamship line. If the Government were entitled to exercise any influence, it might well have been directed against the Canadian Pacific Railway Steamship Company. They were a strong, independent, and powerful railway and steamship company, and if there were any merits in the claims that were being made by the members of the Government for a reversion to the port of St.
John by that steamship line, the Canadian Pacific railway officials were perfectly competent to decide whether that request possessed merits or not. On the other hand, as everybody knows, the Canadian Northern Railway Company have been for years -they were last session and probably will be in the future-suppliants for Government financial favours, and pressure could very easily be exercised, and very unfairly exercised, upon this particular railway company which owned the Royal Line of Steamships. I say that interference by the Government in connection with this matter was objectionable in any event, but particularly when directed against a company who frequently were supplicants for financial aid from this Government and from Parliament.
It is not necessary that I should say much more. It has been urged by the press in St. John and Halifax, and by friends of the Government, that the Royal Line of Steamships adopted the port of St. John because there was not at the port of Halifax sufficient terminal facilities. In answer to that, I have to say that I do not think the facts will substantiate that position. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company were quite satisfied to adopt the port of Halifax, and the head of that steamship company stated that the facilities at the port of Halifax were sufficient for their purposes, while he was not satisfied with the port facilities at St. John. The Canadian Northern railway officials were quite satisfied with the facilities afforded them at the port of Halifax. There was no contention made on the part of anybody, when, and for some time after the four steamship contractors had made a selection of the port of Halifax under the terms of the contract, that the facilities were inadequate or insufficient. In fact, St. John newspapers friendly to the Government, when the selection made by the contracting steamship companies was first announced, declared that in respect to facilities Halifax enjoyed a stronger position than did St. John, although in neither case perhaps were the facilities up to actual requirements. I do not believe for one moment that any evidence will be forthcoming from any of the contracting steamship companies, or from the Government or any members of the Government, to the effect that a change of port was made by the Royal Steamship line of its own volition, without interference and pressure on the part of the Government, or because

they considered that the port facilities at Halifax were inadequate.
I shall repeat two or three facts which are, after all, the salient facts in connection with the, remarks I have been making, and which are most important in connection with the whole matter of the transatlantic winter mail service contracts. When the present contract was entered into a year ago, it was expressly stipulated that the contractors had the right to select their winter port, namely, Halifax or St. John. It was stated by the Postmaster General when announcing this contract to Parliament, and it was stated by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries speaking only in November last in the city of St. John, that this optional feature of the contract would settle the merits of the ports of St. John and Halifax for winter mail service purposes. This feature of the contract was in many respects commendable, and should not have been interfered with by the Government. I say that there was interference on the part of the Government or some of its members; I say the Royal Line of Steamships did make a change in their selection of port because of the intervention of the Government; and I say further, that this intervention was unfair and unjust to the steamship company itself, and to the port of Halifax as well. For this transatlantic mail service, the country was paying $1,000,000 a year. Time was the essence of the contract, and it was in the interests of every portion of Canada that that port should be selected by the contracting steamship companies which gave Canadians their British mails in the quickest time possible. The port which should be selected was that which was quickest for this purpose and which was also the safest. As a member of this House, and as representing a constituency much interested in this matter, I desire to register my protest against the intervention of the Government, and their apparent violation of the spirit of the contract negotiated and entered into by them on behalf of the people of Canada. I am very anxious indeed to hear from some one on behalf of the Government as to the nature and extent of the interference they made in this matter, and the defence therefor. I trust that all the papers in connection with the subject, including the substance of the oral negotiations, will be presented to Parliament for our information.

I am very sorry indeed not to have some

reply vouchsafed by the Minister of Marine, if by no other member of the Cabinet, because this is a matter of great importance to his own constituency; it is probably equally as important to his constituency as it is to the constituency of the Prime Minister. The Minister of Marine knows that we might as well discuss this question here for a little while this afternoon, and try to get all the light we can on the subject, because the end has not yet been heard of this matter in the Maritime provinces. The people in the Maritime provinces do not at the present time understand the true significance of this juggling with business affairs and the great transportation interests of this country, which has been taking place during the last six or eight months between the Government, the Intercolonial railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Steamship Company. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has gone into the matter so exhaustively that it is not my intention to discuss it to any great extent from the standpoint of what took place in Parliament.
I would like, however, to refer to the statement made by the Postmaster General when this matter was before Parliament in the month of April last. I remember very distinctly, when the vote of $1,000,000 for mail subsidies was under consideration, the question being asked, from what port these vessels would sail. The answer was given by the Postmaster General as follows:
Mr. Pelletier: Halifax or St. John, at the option of the contractor, which means that each of the ports will stand on its own merits. We undertake to deliver the mails through whichever of the ports the companies will choose, for both the winter and the summer services.
I am not here to speak for the port of St. John; that is the business of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Neither am 1 here to say a word for or against the port of Halifax; that is the business of the Premier and my hon. friend from Halifax. These three gentlemen are perfectly capable of looking after their own interests. I am here to try to point out to the House and to the country the real sufferer in this unfair and unbusinesslike transaction between the Government and their friends, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway and all the other parties concerned. In my opinion, the real sufferer in this transaction is the Intercolonial railway. As a citizen of this country, as a member of this House, I am interested in the question as to whether or not the Inter-

colonial railway is being properly handled. Coming as I do from the Maritime provinces, I am interested in the matter probably to a greater extent than would be a member from the western portions of Canada. Nevertheless we are all interested, and I think we could very profitably discuss this matter from that standpoint for a few moments.
When I say that about the 3rd or 4th of October last consternation reigned in the city of St. John over this matter, I am stating the case very mildly indeed. The answer given by the Postmaster General in the month of April last, that the steamship companies would have the right to choose whichever port they preferred from business reasons, was absolutely satisfactory to every man in the province of New Brunswick. From the evidence of my hon. friend from Halifax, I believe it was equally satisfactory to the people of Halifax. I am willing to admit that during the last ten or fifteen years there has been far too much bickering, backbiting and saying of unkind things by people in the cities of St. John and Halifax. Too. much parochial politics has been indulged in by the people representing both of the cities-I do not mean by their representatives in this House, but by the people of these communities in general. This country is big enough and there is sufficient business in it to justify a broader stand being taken, and I for one have never been guilty of taking any part in these debates, and I do not think they tend to the benefit of either port or of the country as a whole.
In April last we thought we had finally got down to the business proposition that the steamship companies would be allowed to choose whichever port they thought was the better from a business -standpoint; and both cities apparently were satisfied. I do not want to say anything unkind about any member of the Government, because it does not do any good. The matter is serious enough in itself without my saying anything that will make it more unpleasant or more serious. We in the province of New Brunswick are asking where the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was when this trade was going on. If I understand my hon. friend from Halifax aright this afternoon, he is now asking where the Premier was when the latter trade was made whereby Canadian Northern boats were switched from Halifax to St. John. I must take the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at his word; he is a gentleman whom I know very well and I am satisfied that every person in the province will take the minister at his word. When
this matter first came up, a telegram was sent by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the President of the Board of Trade. The substance of that telegram is that the people of St. John must not get excited over this matter because, as far as the minister knew, there was no intention of taking the Empress steamers away from St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman had
better read the telegram.

This is the telegram. I am reading now from the Daily Telegraph of October 7, 1913:
October 4, 1913.
Dear Mr. Robinson:
I am in receipt of yours of the 3rd instant. I have been very much surprised that the Canadian Pacific railway have decided to send the Empresses to Halifax, and can understand the expressions of disappointment that have been given utterance to. The feeling, however, that undue influence has been used to force the shipping people to this action is absolutely and entirely without any foundation whatever. They are perfectly free agents in the matter. The contract entered into was along the lines which St. John has wanted for so many years, namely, that mails should be delivered to the ships either at Halifax or St. John and that they should be at liberty to use whichever port they pleased.
I am more than surprised at the action in view of the statement attributed to Sir Thomas Shaughnessy to the effect that the Empresses would not call at Halifax at all had they not been compelled to do so. It was unfortunate that when a contract has been entered into in exactly the terms and conditions the people of St. John have so long desired that the result should not have been more satisfactory.
Sir Thomas Shaughnessy wired me yesterday that the Victorian and Virginian, together with all the other Allan and Canadian Pacific railway steamers would go direct from St. John, and that that would he all the steamers that the port could possibly accommodate.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) J. D. Hazen.
Probably that does not refer to the Empresses. My statement then was not probably exact.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Undoubtedly that has
reference to the Empresses.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think so.
I do not think the minister intended to convey to the people ot St. John that the Empresses would go from St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, all the other Canadian Pacific railway steamers, and the Victorian and the Virginian.

That is right.
Two or three days after that a delegation

came from St. John to Ottawa to interview the Government. In view of the statements made in that telegram by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and made to the delegation later on, I am bound to assume that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not know of the agreement that had been made between the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian 'Pacific railway, or what is known in New Brunswick as the Gutelius agreement. I am bound to assume that it was made behind his back, and perhaps he will not consider me discourteous if I say that he did not at that time appreciate the true significance of it after it had been made. If I wanted any evidence of that, I would simply take the statement made by the Eremier himself when a delegation met him in Ottawa, I think on the 9th of October.
The Prime Minister practically told the delegation that he did not know the terms of the agreement; he understood ft had been made, between the two companies but it was purely a business agreement, one into which politics did not enter and in which no members of the Government had taken any part. I do not know that he went so far as to say that no member of the Government had been consulted or considered, but I think we might almost fairly assume that much from the general tenor of his statement to the delegation. Now, if these statements be true-and I give them for what they are worth, and I will allow these hon. gentlemen to explain them as they wish to -we come down to this:	The Canadian
Pacific railway had been coming to St. John with their Empress boats for three, four or five years. They wanted to continue coming to St. John. It was their home port. The waters of St. John harbour had been found deep enough and broad enough to accommodate the Empresses in the past, and there is no evidence, that the waters were more shallow at St. John in 1914 than they were in 1913. Therefore, so far as physical conditions go, there was no reason why the boats should not continue to come. The Victorian and Virginian also had been coming, and there was no reason why they should not continue to come-and it was agreed, I understand, that they should continue to come. The Royal boats had been going to Halifax for three years. They had all the accommodation they wanted, and did not wish any change. The Allan boats had been going to Halifax. I have no strong evidence as to whether they wanted to change or not. As the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, the Cana-

dian Pacific railway had made arrangements and published advertisements of the sailing dates of their steamships from St. John during the winter season. He knows also that they had made contracts in St. John for the delivery of supplies for the whole season. He must know that; or, if he does not know it, he can easily learn it by going to St. John. All arrangements that a steamship company could make had been made for carrying on their business during the season 1913-14. Then, the right hon. Prime Minister knows, the Royal steamships had made arrangements to go from Halifax and wanted to go from Halifax during the winter; it was to their interest to sail to and from Halifax. But suddenly, as if by magic, without anybody asking these people to make the change, the whole thing was turned upside down, the Canadian Pacific railway steamers were sent from St. John to Halifax. And then, in order, as I say, to try to assuage the wrath that was piling up on the head of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Royal steamers were taken away from Halifax and sent to St. John. I say, wrath was being heaped upon the head of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am reminded by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that this feeling of anger and opposition reached such a point that certain members of the Borden Club of St. John resigned their positions. I have here a newspaper clipping giving a copy of the resolution which they passed, and, I think in view of the dissent expressed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to what my hon. friend from Halifax, perhaps I had better read this resolution:
Whereas a great injustice lias been done to the port of St. John by the agreement entered into by the Government railway and the Canadian Pacific railway which agreement plainly discriminates against St. John, in that by it the Canadian Pacific railway is enabled to take away its mail boats, and the mail boats of the Allan line, after they had been advertised to sail from St. John direct, and as the hon. R. L. Borden has stated, that it required the approval of the Minister of Railways before becoming effective, we the undersigned members of the R. I*. Borden club, feeling that the ratification should be refused, wish to resign from any active participation in the affairs of the club until this matter has been settled by the cancellation of the Gutelius and Bosworth agreement. We do this as a protest to show that while we are Conservatives, we cannot support a Government if it persists in carrying out this discrimination agreement.
Mr. W. J. Brown, one of those who signed this resolution, had been the Con-

servative organizer for Kings-Albert. I understand that about twelve or thirteen signed this resolution and resigned. I have not the names at hand. This resolution gives you an idea of the pitch to which feeling had arisen in St. John at this time. This was some time in the month of October-the 29th or 39th, I think. When the delegation came to Ottawa about the 7th or 8th October, the Premier told the delegation that he could not give them the exact terms of the agreement, because it was a matter of business between the two railroads, but that later on would send them a copy of it. My recollection is that the delegation remained here for two or three days, but failed to get anything more than the mere headings of the agreement. They then went to Montreal and saw Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, but got very little satisfaction from him. Now, to bear out the statement which I made a few minutes ago that the Canadian Pacific railway wished to remain in St. John, let me read an extract from the St. John Daily Telegraph, of October 6, in which Sir Thomas Shaughnessy is reported to have made the following statement:
St. John, he remarked, Is the Canadian Pacific's winter port, and traffic handled to and from Halifax is by grace of the Intercolonial railway. The Atlantic mail service during the past few years has been most satisfactory, the call at both Halifax and St. John involved-
I think that should be ' unsatisfactory,' but I read it as it is.
-undue risks to the vessels in making the trip between the two ports along the coast of Nova Scotia in all sorts of weather, and eastbound ' passengers who embarked at St. John were necessarily subjected to a delay at Halifax of from twelve to twenty hours each voyage. The company would have sacrificed its interest in the mail subsidy rather than make the two calls again.
According to that, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy would rather even give up the mail subsidy than to call at these two ports. He wanted the mail contract to come to St. John.
Why did he sign the agreement which took him to Halifax? Can the hon. gentleman explain that ?

I am coming to that. Of course, I can only give my own version of it. Now, the condition of affairs which 1 have been trying to describe-perhaps at a little too great length-was absolutely satisfactory to all the people of St. John, to the people of Halifax, so far as we can see, and to the railway and steamship companies as well. The Royal people
wanted to go to Halifax; the Canadian Pacific railway and the Allans-which I understand are about the same thing- wanted to come to St. John and had all their, arrangements made accordingly. Now, in order to break up that harmonious condition of affairs between all parties, one of the most memorable agreements in the annals of the Intercolonial railway was prepared and signed on the 30th of September, which, I think, we have from an answer given by the Minister of Railways and Canals this afternoon; and while I have not the agreement in full, I have the substance of it as furnished to the delegation from St. John, which I propose to read. I think this must be practically accurate, because it has been published in the newspapers. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has been trying to get the agreement, or a copy of it, ever since this session opened in January, but has failed to do so. Therefore, I do not think the Government can object to my reading the copy furnished the delegation from St. John, which is as follows:
Memorandum of agreement between the Canadian Government Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company covering the transportation of freight and passengers between Halifax and St. John over the Intercolonial railway in connection with the Canadian Pacific and Allan Line steamships, carrying British mails, making Halifax the terminal port (four ships).
The following rates will govern the transportation of passengers:
Passengers and their baggage between Halifax and St. John in either direction, on special or regular trains, $2. first-class, and $1.50 second-class for each adult passenger, with a maximum earning on this traffic on any one train of $300.
It is understood that when special trains are run they shall handle, if necessary, up to twelve cars, making same time as regular through trains.
The Canadian Pacific to supply a reasonable proportion of the necessary equipment and the Intercolonial to undertake without charge such deadhead movements as may be necessary to properly care for the traffic; it being agreed that the Canadian Pacific will not be asked to hold their cars in Halifax for more than seven days at any one time.
The Intercolonial will assume the cost of transfer of baggage between cars and shed floor.
The Intercolonial will pay the same rental and other charges on cars in this service as at present paid on Canadian Pacific equipment handled over the line between St. John and Halifax.
The Canadian Pacific shall pay the same charges for cleaning, supplies, etc., as now paid the Intercolonial.
Freight of all classes, in either direction, 75 cents per ton of 2,000 lb. with the exception of flour and grain which will be carried at the rate of 60 cents per ton of 2,000 lb. The maxi-

mum earning for this traffic on any one train to he $300.
The Canadian Pacific will assume the cost of transferring freight between ships and cars at .Halifax.
All grain handled-*
There are a few words here which I [DOT]cannot make out.
It means all grains 'handled through Halifax elevators.

Yes, and it goes on:
-shall pay the usual elevator charge current at other ports.
The Canadian Pacific will assume the clerical work, checking, way-billing and accounting.
The Intercolonial will pay the usual per diem or other charge on freight car equipment engaged in this business, and also all loss or damage which may occur to the freight while in transit between Halifax and St. John.
The Intercolonial will provide the necessary berthing accommodation for the Canadian Pacific and Allan Ijine ships, and will make no greater charge for wharfage and dockage dues than is charged other steamship lines.
This arrangement will remain in effect from November 15, 1913, to May 15, 1914.
Sgd. G. M. Bosworth,
for Canadian Pacific railway.
F. P. Gutelius,
Canadian Government railways.
Montreal, September 30, 1913.
We have to analyse this agreement in order to see the unfair treatment which has been accorded the Intercolonial railway and the city of St. John. It is hard to figure out what it is costing the Government or the country to handle this traffic, but it is very clear that the Canadian Pacific railway is not paying the Intercolonial railway anything like what it Actually costs to handle the traffic-unless all statistics as to the cost of railway transportation which have been given out by railway officials in the past are absolutely false and absurd, and unless freight and passengers can be hauled on railway trains for about one-half or one-third the amount we have been led to believe they *can be hauled for. We find that passengers going from St. John to Halifax, or vice -versa, shall pay $2 a head for first-class [DOT] and $1.50 for second-class accommodation. The distance is 275 miles. I do not know -what the rate would actually be, but putting it at two cents a mile-and the ,hon. member for South York (Mr. McLean) [DOT]can tell me whether or not the Intercolonial railway is giving a two-cent rate-the rate one way would be $5.50, and the Government are hauling Canadian Pacific railway first-class passengers for $2 and second-class passengers for $1.50. If the matter stopped there, it would be bad enough, but 
nothing like as bad as it is, because it is expressly agreed that the Government railway shall haul trains up to twelve cars in a train, and that the total cost of that train shall not exceed $300. We know that the average railway car to-day, such as is used by the Canadian Pacific railway on through trains, carries at least 75 and perhaps 100 people. I refer not to Pullman cars, but to first-class and second-class coaches. At the rate of only 60 passengers to a car, a train consisting of ten passenger cars and two baggage cars would carry 600 passengers, and at that rate you are only getting fifty cents a passenger instead of $2. If 300 passengers are carried, you are getting only $1 a passenger, because, although it is agreed that the rate shall be $2 a passenger, it is stipulated that the maximum earning on any one train shall be $300. When 5 p.m. you read it in that light, you commence to see some of the remarkable conditions of this agreement in so far as passenger traffic is concerned. When you come to the question of freight the conditions are equally as bad, if not worse. The freight rate, the agreement says, shall be seventy-five cents a ton of two thousand pounds, but the same conditions prevail; the total cost to the Canadian Pacific railway on any train shall not exceed $300. I am not sufficiently versed in the doings of the Intercolonial railway to tell exactly how much freight they can handle, but I do know something about railway transportation, and I think I am well within the mark when I say that the average Intercolonial engine- what we call the 100 or 125 per cent engine -will haul at least 600 tons from Halifax to St. John. This 600 tons of freight is hauled for $300; instead of getting seventy-five cents the Government is getting only fifty cents a ton for hauling this freight. Except over heavy grades, such as the Folly Mountain, where a pusher might be required for a short distance, there is no reason why the larger engines running between St. John and Halifax should not haul 700, 800 or 900 tons to a train. If as much as 900 tons are taken on a train, they are getting 900 tons hauled for $300-about thirty cents a ton; and if you take the ordinary moderate estimate of 600 tons to a train, they get this freight hauled for fifty cents a ton. It would be interesting, I am sure, if any hon. gentleman in this House, particularly the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, would take up the freight schedules of the Intercolonial

railway and see how far out of St. John he can have a ton of freight hauled on the Intercolonial railway for fifty cents. I am sure he would be amused to find what a short distance his freight would be hauled for that amount. But, if you take a carload of freight weighing say 30 tons-I think that is about the average-at fifty cents, the cost of hauling that carload of freight from St. John to Halifax would be $15. I wonder whether my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries could have a carload of freight hauled from St. John to Hampton, a distance of some twenty-five miles, for $15. I tell him he could not, and I tell him further that he could not have that carload of freight hauled to Rothesay, a distance of twelve miles, for $15; yet this freight is being hauled to Halifax, a distance of 275 miles, at the rate of about $15 a car. That is not all. In this agreement it is agreed that the Intercolonial will
Undertake without charge such deadhead movements as may be necessary to properly care for the traffic.
In ordinary language that means that they will bring back the empties free of charge. We do not know what proportion of those cars that go to Halifax will come back as empties, but we know that there will be a large number; we know that the outward freight is probably double or treble the inward freight. I think I am right in saying that probably one-half of these cars come back deadheads. I have made inquiries of competent railway officials, and I find that the railway companies can hardly distinguish the difference in cost between hauling an empty car and a full car. A little more coal may be used in hauling the full car, but all the other charges are practically the same. Even the extra coal may be offset by the fact that the train is longer in the case of empties, and that there is more wind resistance to be overcome. So you are hauling one-half of these cars back as deadheads, which will cost as much as hauling loaded cars. Even that is not all. They actually agreed to pay the ordinary per diem allowance for cars, the rental just as they would pay under other circumstances. I think the rate now is 35 cents a day. That is, if the Canadian Pacific railway hands a car over to the Intercolonial railway, the Intercolonial railway has to pay 35 cents per day until the car is returned to the owning company. This ear of freight goes to Halifax and it is at least ten days before it gets back to St.
John. Then there is a payment of $3.50, which the Intercolonial railway pays to the Canadian Pacific railway for the use of that car in hauling that freight practically for nothing.
Let us come back to the passengers. They say that passengers and baggage between St. John and Halifax will be carried on special or regular trains for $2 first-class and $1.50 second-class. I do not know how that wiil work out, because if they are carrying passengers on regular trains, as I figure out, if the regular train earns more than $300 between St. John and Halifax, the Canadian Pacific railway get the benefit of that on whatever proportion of passengers they may have between St. John and Halifax; so you might conceive an instance of the Intercolonial railway hauling passengers for nothing if you had sufficient regular business on the regular train. But I want to be fair, and I assume that the majority of these passengers will be handled in through trains. There might be many cases when a carload of immigrants would be attached to a regular train. As I understand it, you might assume a condition where the Canadian Pacific railway passengers would be actually hauled free of charge, and not only that but the Intercolonial railway would be actually paying rental for the car in which they travelled. This is the means by which they have been able to switch from St. John the traffic which rightly belongs to it. I do not believe, nor does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the Minister of Railways, that they can handle this trarffic at the price put down here. If you can haul a carload of freight from St. John to Halifax for $15 and bring that car back empty and pay 35 cents a day for that car while you are doing it, I cad only say that the railway companies of this country have been robbing the people to an extent such as we never dreamed of before. But I do not propose to take that ground; I do not propose to say that the railway companies have charged much more than they should. Possibly the rates could be pared down a great deal and yet the railways could pay dividends; but there cannot be any such fearful difference in the actual cost of carrying freight and the rate the railways have been charging, as will be found in this Gutelius agreement.
In the newspapers and in Parliament, since the 7th of October last, we have been' trying to ascertain the actual cost of carrying these trains, and the Government will

not vouchsafe one particle of evidence. Therefore I am bound to assume, from my little horse .sense and knowledge of railway matters, that they are carrying this traffic at an immense loss. The result is that St. John is losing the business which naturally belongs to it, and the city of Halifax, in order to get around the political difficulties, was compelled to lose business which actually belonged to it. The Canadian Northern, as we all know, do not route their freight over the Canadian Pacific railway through the state of Maine; they do not want to. They want to utilize the Intercolonial from Montreal, and they are doing so, and they want to send their freight from Montreal to Halifax. They want to use Halifax as their port; but, in order to meet the political exigencies of hon. gentlemen-and here I may say the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because he did get into the worst hole any man ever did in the province- in order to meet the political exigencies of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, they switched the traffic that actually belonged to Halifax away from it; and, in order to meet the political exigencies of the Premier, they switched from the port of St. John the traffic which actually belonged to it, and the Intercolonial railway is carrying that freight for one-half what it costs to operate it, let alone deriving any profit. Sir Thomas Shaughnessy said that this agreement was only made possible by the grace of the Intercolonial railway. If the Intercolonial railway did not haul this freight for less than it cost to do iso, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy -would not have taken advantage of it, and if he had not done so this switching of traffic would not have taken place.
Coming to the very pertinent question propounded by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who wants to know why in my opinion all this was done if the railway companies did not want it and St. John and Halifax did not want it, I may say that if I gave the answer which was in my mind some of my friends might not consider it parliamentary. But I leave him to draw the only inference that can be drawn. I ask him if he believes Mr. Gute-lius was allowed to make this one-sided agreement, so inimical to the best interests of the Intercolonial railway, without the knowledge and consent of the Government or at least of certain members of it. Has my hon. friend sufficient imagination to believe that that would have taken place? I cannot make myself believe that Mr. 
Gutelius or any other manager of the Intercolonial railway would make a contract such as this without some one giving him the wink and saying: Go ahead now, you cannot make it too strong for us. It is not possible; it is not reasonable. If I am right in my suggestions, is it not most remarkable that the Intercolonial railway, the one great public asset of the people of eastern 'Canada, has been prostituted in order to carry out or help smooth over the political exigencies of certain members of the Government?-because there is no other conclusion.
There is another side to this question. I was surprised in looking over the railway statistics recently brought	down-I had
only a hurried glance at them- to find that the Intercolonial railway was run at a loss last year of something like over $250,000. We were led to believe, during the last session of Parliament, that there was going to be a great surplus of about half a million dollars; but I am told that there was an actual loss. If that is the case, what is going to be the result this year? Oh, but, they say, we are going to have more revenue this year. They are hauling Canadian Pacific railway freight for one-quarter to one-third of what it actually costs, in order to play the political game of my friends opposite and in order to make up for that they have increased the freight rates from Montreal to Sydney.
Hear, hear.

There is not a
member here representing a Maritime constituency, let him be Liberal or Conservative, but will say ' hear, hear ' to that statement. Things got so bad that two or three members supporting the Government threatened to resign if something were not done to ameliorate the condition of affairs thrust upon the people by the action of Mr. Gutelius.
Where is the Minister of Railways?

does no apply to my department. I do not know very much about it except this: the Canadian Pacific railway had occasion to speak to me in connection with my department, about this contract to which my hon. friend has referred, and far from being under the impression that this was a very bad bargain for the Intercolonial railway, which the hon. member for Carleton has tried to convey to the House, the Canadian Pacific railway were under the impression that if that bargain did not cover mail transportation they had made a very bad bargain for themselves. The question came up in connection with the special trains to take the mails from Halifax. The Canadian Pacific railway pretended they were entitled to handle those mails on their trains from Halifax to Montreal. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I gave the preference to our own railway.

We know that in New
Brunswick.
I suppose that is another complaint which my hon. friend has. Let him bring it up and I will deal with it to his satisfaction, which is not a very easy thing to do.
One thing at a time.

Yes. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. The contract for the carrying of the mails from Halifax to Montreal was given to the Intercolonial railway, and then the Canadian Pacific railway complained very bitterly and very loudly. They said the contract should have been given to them, under the arrangement which has been referred to. Finally, however, the Intercolonial railway got the contract. The complaint by the Canadian Pacific railway was that they had made a very bad bargain indeed, if they did not have the right to carry the mails from Halifax to Montreal. However, I need not discuss the merits of the agreement entered into. I have been very much impressed with the speeches made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) whom I see now sitting side by side. I never saw such a case of riding two horses, and, at the same time, riding two horses going in opposite directions, as these two gentlemen have performed today. It was a most wonderful performance.
Was it well done?

It was pretty well
done, but I think it is being carried to such length that the people will understand it before long. These hon. gentlemen surely cannot have any reasonable expectation that the people of Canada will be fooled by the diverse attitudes taken by these two deskmates, one saying you have done wrong to Halifax, and another say-iing: you have done wrong to St. John. How could an injustice be done to St. John by the steamships going there, and at the same time an injustice be done to Halifax by the steamships using that port? However, my hon. friend from St. John says that what was done was wrong, and my hon. friend from Halifax says the same thing, so that an ordinary individual will find it pretty difficult to recognize the consistency of the attitude taken by these hon. gentlemen.	-
Argue the question and never mind that.

I am trying to find out what these hon. gentlemen mean, because in order to argue the point they attempt to make, I must first know what their point is. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) says: 'You have taken away the steamships from Halifax to bring them to St. John.'
I say you violated your contract.
I say so too.
Then, when the hon. member for Halifax takes his seat, the hon. member for Carleton rises and says: 'You have wronged St. John.' Which of the two are we to believe?
Both.
That is just the kind of policy pursued by my right hon. friend.
You are wrong both ways.

The right hon. gentleman- puts two absolutely opposite policies before the country and he tells the people that they must take stock in both of them. We have been told by the hon. member for Halifax and by the hon. member for Carleton, that we entered into a contract which they both agree was eminently fair, for they tell us that the contract which was made by the four steamship companies gave the ports of Halifax and St. John a chance to stand on their own merits, and they say further that every person in Nova Scotia

and New Brunswick was satisfied with that provision. I want to say that we have lived up to that contract. When I submitted the contract to the House, I stated that the companies objected very strongly to calling at both ports, because they said, it was a most dangerous and expensive voyage. They said we will go to one port, but we will not call at both. It was then provided that the steamship companies should call at whichever port they saw fit', provided it was a Canadian port, this being the only restriction which I, as Postmaster General, put in the. contract. We are told by these hon. gentlemen opposite to-day that this was an eminently fair proposition. But can either of these hon. gentlemen contend for a moment that this contract has been changed? It has not been changed. It stands to-day just as it stood when it was entered into.

The minister says the contract has not been changed and that the companies have gone to the port they selected. Will he say that neither the Government, nor any member of the Government, used pressure on the Canadian Northern Railway Company to change from Halifax to St. John ?
If the hon. member will allow me to make my statement, he will not find it necessary to ask such a question.
I only wanted to have the views of the minister on that point.

My statement now is that the contracts have not been changed since they were signed; they are contracts only for the current year up to the first of May next. The companies were allowed, under the contract, to choose whatever port they wished. If there has been trouble over the matter it is due*to a fact to which neither the hon. member for Halifax nor the hon. member for Carleton has referred, and which (while I do not want to unduly criticise any one), provoked a most unhappy situation. When the contract was entered' into, I said to the contractors: I will state in the House that the ports are going to stand on their respective merits; that you can make your selection of either, and I did so. Then, at a given moment, when every one believed that each port would be given a fair test and a fair chance to stand on its own merits, the announcement was made that all the ships were going to St. John. This fact has not been referred to by either of the hon. gentlemen opposite, but they know it to be true.
Do you say that all the ships are going to St. John ?
Yes, every one of them.
I never heard of that.

Who made
that announcement?
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and the Allans.
We understood that the. Canadian Pacific railway and the Allans were going to St. John, but not the Canadian Northern ships.
I am not referring to, the Royals now.
Nor the White Star.

I refer to the an, nouncement made about all the big ships;: the Alsatian and the Calgarian were ex-, pected to be on the route and they were to go to St. John as also the Empresses, and the Victorian, and Virginian. There was no announcement made so far as the Royals are concerned. One fine morning this announcement was made to the public in St. John. I am not blaming any one for doing it, but I do say that it created, trouble, and that all the trouble to which, the hon. gentlemen opposite have referred, originated at that point. We found these contractors, using the full liberty they had-under their contract, at a given moment changing their minds, and instead of all the steamers going to Halifax it was an-, nounced they were all going to St. John,
You were awfully surprised, were you not?

I was awfully surprised, because I did not think it was fair treatment of the people. I say so now on the floor of the House, and I told the interested parties it was unfair for the steamship companies to let the people of St. John think they were going there, and then have men like the hon. member for, Carleton (Mr. Carvell) rising in this House, as he did to-day, and saying that if was the Government that was responsible for what occurred. We knew, considering the kind of political warfare that was being carried on, that we would be told, as we were told this afternoon, that we had power over the contractors to make them do as we wished. The Government were.

no party to the change in any way, shape or form.
The companies had -the power to select their port?
Certainly.

What was the
trouble, then?

The trouble was that they had advertised that they were going ito St. John, and then in twenty-four or forty-eight hours they changed their minds completely and stated that they were going to Halifax.

Amongst whom
would that make trouble, and what was the nature of the trouble?

The nature of the
trouble should be very easily understood by a clever gentleman like my hon. friend from Halifax. Supposing the companies had advertised publicly that they were all going [DOT]to Halifax, and the people of Halifax had been very much pleased over this, and then within forty-eight hours after the people of Halifax had had this good news, the companies changed their minds and all decided to go to St. John; would not the people of Halifax be disappointed. It stands to reason they would.

That is what
happened?

That is what happened in St. John. The companies, after advertising publicly that they would go to St. John, changed their minds two or three days afterwards and, instead of having all their fine ships, the Alsatian, the Calgarian, the Victorian, the Virginian -and the Empresses *going to St. John as advertised, and after having made a timetable for St. John, they -decided to go to Halifax. This was done without the intervention of the Government, in any way, shape or form. It has created the regrettable situation which now exists, and I have had occasion to tell the people who did it what I thought of them. It was done, however. After all this took place, the Royal boats, seeing that all these other ships were going to Halifax, decided to go to St. John. No undue pressure nor undue influence was brought to bear on the Royal line to go either to St. John or to Halifax.

What kind of
influence was it if it was not undue influence? Will the hon. minister describe what influence was exercised?
Well, I cannot describe a thing which does not exist. My hon. friend will have to live a few years longer before he tries to catch me with such a question as that.
I was not trying to catch the hon. gentleman.
I was not born a few years ago.
It is information that we are after.
None of the steamship companies which have entered into this contract has been forced by my department to change the terms of its contract or to enter into a new contract.

Will the hon.
minister deny that he had interviews with the Canadian Northern Steamship Company on this matter?

I will not deny that 1 had interviews with all these railway companies and steamship companies in regard to this matter. I told them what I thought of this advertising which was changed later on and stated that it created a regrettable situation. My hon. friend would have done the same thing had he been in my place. No undue influence or pressure, however, was exercised to bring to Halifax vessels which were going to St. John. If it were true that the Government had taken the Empresses from St. John to put them into Halifax and had taken the Royals from Halifax to put them into St. John, we would have done a thing which would have compensated itself, but we would have created trouble for ourselves to no purpose. The Royals havt been'going to St. John under the terms of the agreement which has been signed and which has not been changed.
The whole situation can be summed up in the following way: Our friends, the Liberals in St. John, say that we are interfering in favour of Halifax, and the Liberals in Halifax say that we are interfering in favour of St. John. They are trying to create local prejudice in both cities against the Government, whereas the Government is trying to inaugurate a great public service in the interest of the country at large. They go to the city of St. John and say: Look at this Government; they are doing this for Halifax and they should do it for St. John. They go to the city of Halifax and say:	Look at this
Government; they are doing this for St.

John and they should do it for Halifax. The Liberals are doing this in order to create local prejudice and they expect the people to believe that the Government is doing these things. I have been disappointed at the way in which this matter has been treated. We have tried to give a good service to Canada. We are disappointed in some respects on account of the <Alsatian and the Calgarian not being in service last summer. We hope to be able to improve the service next year, and have strong reasons to believe that we are going to do so. I think, however, that every member of this House should help us to make this a great public service rather than a question in which petty local prejudice will take first place and first rank.

If I understood my hon. friend aright, he said that all the trouble in this matter came from the fact that Canadian Pacific Railway Company, after having advertised that they would take their ships to St. John, within forty-eight hours changed their minds and decided to go to Halifax instead.
I would not like to say that it was within forty-eight hours, but it was two or three or four days afterwards.

That is not my point. The important point is this, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, after having stated to the people at St. John and to the country that their ships would go to St. John, changed their minds within a short time and said that they would take them to Halifax. Can my hon. friend explain how it is that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would have acted in that way? What was their reason for so doing?

I cannot state what
was their reason, but I told them that it was not fair treatment to the people of St. John to tell them they were going there, and then a few days later to change their minds, thus creating trouble for us. I did not mince matters with them. They said they thought it was in the interest of the company to make the change and they had done it. That is the answer I got.
Was it before the 30th of September, 1913, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company announced that they were going to St. John, and did they change their minds after the 30th of September?

I could not say
whether it was after or before, because I only came back from the West on the 30th of September. My recollection of the matter is what was stated to us at an interview which the citizens of St. John had with my right hon. friend the leader of the Government. I was present at that interview which took place about the beginning of October. They made the statement that these advertisements had been sent out by the Allan Line and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. After the meeting was over I went to these gentlemen and said that I would like them to show me these advertisements so that I could say that I had seen them. That is what justified me in speaking in regard to the matter later on.
Just because advertisements had been sent out?
Because advertisements had been sent out and made known to the public.
You think that that is important?
Yes, I do.

My friend has not left it quite clear in my mind, but I understand that he comes to the conclusion, from what certain gentlemen from St. John told him, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company changed their minds within two or three days. Did he afterwards get the information from the Canadian Pacific railway, that they had changed their minds?

I heard it in the first instance from the gentlemen who came here on the deputation. I think that the advertisements were published some time towards the end of September, when I was away in the West. I remember coming back to Ottawa on the 30th of September, and that interview took place some time in October. Then for the first time I heard that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Allan Company had done this.

The minister has not
caught the point. Did he afterwards get information from the Canadian Pacific railway themselves that they had changed their minds?

Yes. I put it up to the Canadian Pacific railway. I said: Why did you do that? They said they thought it in the interest of their own company, and



the contract, they said, allowed them to change their port.

speakeroldname: Bt. Hon. E. L. BOEDEN (Prime Minister) :
speechtext: As I may not have an opportunity to speak this evening, I would like to say a word on this subject in the short time allowed before the House rises. The facilities provided in the way of terminals both at Halifax and St. John have not been adequate in recent years for the traffic. In both cities new terminals are being constructed, and it is hoped that, within a very short time, at both these ports terminals will be provided which will enable them to handle traffic at least on equal terms with any other port on the Atlantic, or any port elsewhere in the world. The contract to which my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) has referred left it open to each company to select the port from which it should sail. I did not personally conduct the negotiations, but I understood that there was a decided objection on the part of the companies to having their ships call at both ports. ' The desire was that they should call at one port or the other; and we left it entirely open to the companies to select the port from which they should sail. Now the hon. gentlemen who have brought this matter forward have stated the terms of the contract and have said that by reason of some supposed action of the Government the contract has had a certain result. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) who made the motion, endeavours to create the impression that the result operates a3 a discrimination againt Halifax; and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) who seconded the motion endeavours to make it appear that the result is a discrimination against St. John.
I did not argue that.

That is the direct inference, as I understand it, from what my hon. friend has said; for he complained, in the course of his remarks, that certain steamships which formerly called at Halifax did not now call at Halifax but called at St. John. He attributed that result to the interference of the Government. But the gentleman who seconded the motion complains that certain steamships which formerly called at St. John now call at Halifax, and he, in his turn, attributed that result to the action of the Government. 1 do not think I have characterized the conduct of either of these gentlemen in terms to which he can take exception. So far as we were concerned, we left it open

to these companies to select their own ports. A certain amount of discussion has arisen in Halifax and in St. John with regard to the action taken by the respective steamship companies. They were at perfect liberty under the terms of this contract to select the port from which they should sail, and the Government had no means, so far as I am aware, of compelling them or inducing them to go to either one port or the other. I have observed that it has been freely stated in the press which supports hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that some inducement was offered by the Government to one or the other of these companies to take the course they did take. I desire to say that any such statement or insinuation is absolutely without foundation. So far as concerns the terms of the arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway, which my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), who seems to be something of a railway expert, considers absolutely unfair to the Intercolonial railway, the general manager of the Intercolonial railway never had any suggestion or instruction from any member of the Government, so far as I am aware

and certainly not from myself-to make any contract which was not fair and just and equitable to the Intercolonial railway on business terms. And when my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., undertakes to say that the terms are not fair to the Intercolonial railway, I do not propose to set myself up as a railway expert, but I would like to say to him that a little knowledge in these matters, as in some other matters, may occasionally be found a dangerous thing. It was perfectly agreeable to the Government that the terms of this contract should be submitted to the Board of Bailway Commissioners for Canada, and it was suggested, when complaint wras made in regard to the terms that these terms should be submitted, ibut no effective step in that direction has been taken from that time to the present, because, as I understand it, it was not desired to press tiie proposal to that extent.
What would be the user
I do not know what my hon. friend suggests by that question.
The contract was made and the ships had gone to Halifax; what was the use of the people of St. John bothering about the Eailway Commission?

The contract made might be modified. It was made only for six

months. But it was perfectly agreeable to the Government to have the terms examined by any railway expert. It was suggested that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada should be empowered to do so. My hon. friend says they have no jurisdiction. But they could be given jurisdiction, if necessary, by this Parliament, to investigate any such matter. I am not familiar with the terms of the contract. The hon. gentleman states that as I understand it, that the sum of $15 per car was fixed-
That is the way it figures out-$300 a train.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He calculates the rate at $15 a car from Halifax to St. John; and he declares this rate to be so absurd that it cannot be regarded as a business contract.
I am a^guming twenty cars to the train, and that at $300 to the train, makes $15 a car.
That is not the agree ment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

But I will tell him what the Minister of Railways in the late Government put before this House as a reasonable cost for the carriage of cars of wheat and grain from Montreal to Halifax, the distance being estimated at 828 miles. It was hauled at 2 15 cents per bushel. And it was stated in answer to a question by that minister on that occasion that the estimated cost per bushel for the service operated by the Intercolonial railway was 2-27 cents per bushel.

What is my
hon. friend reading from?

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman, neglects this point: In the agreement with Sutherland no maximum amount to be collected was mentioned; whereas in the agreement referred to on this occasion there is a maximum amount of $300.
Not for freight trains,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am dealing only with the point brought up by the hon. member for Carleton, namely, that the charge of $15 for the haulage of a car from St. John to Halifax was so absolutely absurd that the agreement should not be called a business agreement. I would point out that on the same basis the Intercolonial railway, for hauling a car from Montreal to Halifax, should have received more than $45 instead of $13.62 or $22.70.

I would call the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that the freight charges on the Intercolonial railway from here to Halifax are-governed by the mileage on the Canadian Pacific, a competing road, and not by its own mileage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am dealing with the point raised by the hon. member for Carleton, and that point .only. I do not profess to be an expert in these matters, as the hon. member for Westmorland is .said to be, and as the hon. member for Carleton claims to be. The assertion wae made that the price of $15 a car from Halifax to St. John was so absurd tbathe agreement could not be called & business agreement. I am pointing out that: in the answer which was given Dy a member of the late Administration it was stated that a much lower rate was a reasonable charge for hauling a car from Montreal to Halifax,, a distance of 828 miles, and therefore I would be inclined to doubt the absolute knowledge of my hon. friend from Carleton with regard to the subject.
I think that the interests of the country may, perhaps, be safely left in the hands of the gentleman who is at present the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, and who is familiar with these matters -certainly more familiar with them than any hon. gentleman in this House can claim to be. So far .as the Government was concerned, the object and desire was to provide a better steamship service across the Atlac-.

tic and a more speedy conveyance of the mails. In doing that, for the reasons which have been adduced by the railway companies themselves, we left it open to these railway and steamship companies to select their own port. It has happened that two of the Canadian Pacific boats which formerly went to St. John now go to Halifax, and that two of the Canadian Northern boats which formerly went to Halifax now go to St. John. That was a matter over which the Government had no control; that was a matter which under the terms of the contract was absolutely open to the railway and steamship companies themselves to settle-[DOT] and they did settle it accordingly. Even upon the assumption put forward by the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who have discussed this subject, I do not consider that there has been any detriment up to the present time to the interests of either port. I entirely concur in what my hon. friend the Postmaster General has said, that it is not a desirable thing in this House to stir up and dwell upon local animosities or jealousies, but that the two ports, Halifax and St. John, should work together for a common purpose, namely, that of keeping, as far as may be reasonably possible, Canadian traffic, increasing as it is by leaps and bounds from year to year, for our own ports and our own transportation companies.

Of course there is no objection to the papers in this matter being produced, but I decidedly object to that part of the motion in which we are called upon to bring down conversations. We have no detectaphones in our department.
Lucky for you.
I suppose my hon. friend will not mind my asking him to amend his motion to that effect?

I do not see why the hon. Postmaster General should not tell the House the substance of the personal interviews held between himsejf and officials of the Canadian Northern railway. I know that such interviews did take place.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) and my right hon. friend the leader of the Government (Mr. Borden), in dealing with 
this matter, have confined themselves entirely to contending that this is a difficulty between two maritime cities and that the discussion of it is for the purpose of arraying the one against the other; and the Postmaster General, with a dexterity which is characteristic of him, dealt with it purely from that standpoint. I am not concerned with that aspect of the question. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has dealt with it from this standpoint, that the Government had dealt with the matter not merely to the detriment of the city of St. John or the city of Halifax, but had dealt with it unfairly and unjustifiably in affecting and changing the terms of a contract, which had been entered into by the Government of Canada with respect to the carriage of mail. The hon. member for Carleton, N. B., (Mr. Carvell), was not seeking to array one city against the other. He was pointing out distinctly that the Government was doing a wrong to the Intercolonial railway and thereby injuring the interests of Canada at large, in doing as they did-bringing influence to bear to change, in the one instance, the terminals of the Canadian Pacific railway mail steamships, and, in the other instance, the terminals of the Canadian Northern mail steamships. I am interested in the discussion of this matter solely from the standpoint of the way in which it deals with and treats the Intercolonial railway. I think that this contract that was entered into between Mr. Gutelius as representative of the Intercolonial railway and Mr. Bosworth as representing the interests of the Canadian Pacific railway is one of the most outrageous contracts ever entered into between railway companies and one that never would have been entered into by two private corporations. I am sorry the Minister of Railways is not in his seat else I would remind him that last session he came down to the House and told of securing Mr. Gutelius upon a two years' contract at the rate of $20,000 a year; he said that he had secured his services as manager of the Intercolonial railway for that period, that he was so im-' port ant a railway man and was considered as having such great qualifications that the Canadian Pacific railway had merely lent him to the Government for two years in order that he could serve the interests of the Intercolonial railway. We find that after he was engaged as general manager of the Intercolonial railway he entered into this contract, an old employee of the Canadian Pacific railway, for the time being in the employment of the Intercolonial

railway, which lailway paid his salary- he entered into a eon tract with the Canadian Pacific railway with respect to traffic rates over the Intercolonial railway. If my right hon. friend the Prime Minister were in his seat I would ask him if it was true, as stated in the Halifax Herald, during September last, that he called upon Sir Thomas S-haugh-nessy and made the request of him that Halifax should be made the Atlantic terminal port for their steamships. It was so stated in the Halifax Herald and it was so represented, that Mr. Borden as leader of the Government and representing the city of Halifax, went to the Canadian Pacific railway, as represented by Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, and requested that this be done, that Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy's answer was that he could not make Halifax the terminal point when he had St. John fixed for that purpose and that it would entail too serious a loss to the Canadian Pacific railway to change the terminal point and to go to Halifax instead of St. John, and that unless the loss was assumed by the Intercolonial railway he would not make such a change. That is a report of an incident which appears in the Halifax Herald, which certainly is not unfriendly to this Government or to the right hon. gentleman who leads it. We only have the circumstances as a guide to the interpretation of the change that was made. Now it is represented on behalf of the Canadian Pacific railway that going to Halifax would entail a very serious loss to them in the transportation of their freight and passengers to such a distance, particularly in the case of freight. It is recognized that the distance between Montreal and Halifax by way of St. John over the Canadian Pacific railway is shorter than the route over the Intercolonial railway and if the contention of the Canadian Pacific railway, as represented by Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, is correct, that they could not carry their freight to Halifax except at a loss and. that that loss must be assumed by the Intercolonial if he was to be induced to go to Halifax over the rails of the Intercolonial railway, then it must be assumed also that by the longer haul, the greater mileage from Montreal to Halifax, the Intercolonial railway has been sustaining a very serious loss in its export business from Montreal to the port of Halifax. Herein we are face to face with this condition that the Intercolonial railway, if it is true that a loss is incurred by reason of using Halifax as a terminal
point, must assume the burden of its own loss and at the same time, by this agreement, assume the burden of the loss of the Canadian Pacific railway. Evidently the Canadian Pacific railway insisted that the. loss should be borne by the Government through the Intercolonial railway. The agreement entered into is evidence of that fact.
