It is only a temporary agreement.

I care not if it were only for one week. I say that the Minister of Railways himself could not enter into such an arrangement, much less could his general manager acting under him, and therefore it seems to me that while they are operating under this 'agreement they are doing it illegally, against the authority of the law. They must know with respect to the matter. I think my right hon. friend the leader of the Government and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries treated somewhat cavalierly the delegation from St. John. I think that their promise, that they should have the full text of the agreement-which has never been implemented-was just a piece of jollying. I am sorry to come to that conclusion, but I am bound to do so, and I think my right hon. friend in dealing with this matter this afternoon in this House was not treating the House in the way he should. He was not dealing with this matter seriously. He must know that the agreement is not a legal agreement and not binding; he must know that the Government of Canada cannot, His Majesty the King cannot, legally recover any freight charges made under that agreement. The Minister of Railways repudiated the idea that $300 was the maximum charge on a freight train which might contain 30 cars or 50 cars, between St. John and Halifax, but he admitted that $300 was the maximum charge on a 12 car

passenger train. Let me point out to him that the agreement says:
Freight of all classes in either direction 75 cents per ton of 2,000 lbs, with the exception of flour and grain which will be carried at the rate of 60 cents per ton of 2,000 lbs; the maximum earning for this trafflc on any one train to be $300.
It is hot unusual that freight trains between St. John and Halifax may consist of 30 cars, or 40 cars, and even 50 cars; it is largely dependent upon the capacity of the cars hauled and the power of the locomotive used, and yet it is clear that $300 is the maximum charge no matter what the size of the train. I do not think it is opportune for me now to discuss the financial features of this arrangement, but there is no doubt that here we have an arrangement entered into between the Government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific railway, an arrangement not authorized by the Government by Order in Council but carried into effect by their servant and subordinate, and an arrangement which entails upon the Government of Canada the enormous burden of hauling between St. John and Halifax heavily loaded freight trains for the munificent sum of $300. This agreement involves further, the carrying of these empty cars back to St. John without -charge; it involves the payment to the Canadian Pacific railway of a per diem and wheelage allowance on the use of these cars, because the Intercolonial railway is compelled to pay wheelage on these empty cars. What a magnificent contract! Can there be found for it a parallel in America or in the entire railway world? Can there be found anywhere on this continent a like arrangement between any two railway companies? It is not necessary for me to discuss the ulterior motives, if any, the parties had in executing such an arrangement; it only rests with me to state the facts. But, Sir, it involves more than the payment of a merely nominal charge for the carrying of this freight and passenger traffic between St. John and Halifax; it involves the cancellation of trains all over the Intercolonial railway. And why do I say this? I say it because in order to carry out the agreement entered into with the Canadian Pacific railway, the Intercolonial railway, short as it is of motive power, have been compelled to discontinue ordinary trains and take away locomotives for the transportation of special trains for the Canadian Pacific railway between Halifax and St. John. And all this has to be done on account of this nominal remuneration paid to the Intercolonial railway. More than that, and I have proof of the fact, the Intercolonial railway trains are held up repeatedly in order to allow the special trains of the Canadian Pacific railway to have the right of way, the Intercolonial railway trains being subordinated to the convenience of the Canadian Pacific railway trains. Not later than Saturday last, an important train to the business interests of that section of the country represented by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), the train known as No. 83, running from Springhill to Moncton daily except Sunday, was filled with passengers, among them many from Amherst going westwards, and that train was held up for 27 minutes at Aulec station to suit the convenience of a Canadian Pacific railway special running under the terms of this agreement. That same train on the same day was held up for 20 minutes at Sackville, in order to accommodate another Canadian Pacific railway train, so that the large number of passengers on the Intercolonial railway train were delayed 47 minutes to suit the convenience of the Canadian Pacific railway.
But that is not all. The Intercolonial railway trains have been disarranged and cancelled to the disadvantage of the employees of the Intercolonial railway, and to their loss and damage. I am amazed that hon. members from the Maritime provinces, who support the Government knowing as they must know the inconvenience and loss and damage to the people of the Maritime provinces, do not protest against this agreement. It is not too late yet for them to protest. The Government has not ratified the agreement by Order in Council; they have been shielding themselves behind Mr. Gutelius; and who is Mr. Gutelius? I do not know that he is even a Canadian. At one time, I know that he was an importation from the United States, and he came to the Intercolonial railway after he had attempted certain work in connection with the Transcontinental railway, and perhaps we will have the evidence of that work this week as promised by the Minister of Railways. He came to the Maritime provinces and took charge of the Intercolonial. With what effect? With this effect that to-day there is not a man who has been trained on the Intercolonial holding a responsible position on the Intercolonial. The head of the department of maintenance and way, the head of the engineering department, the head of every responsible department of the Intercolonial, who heretofore have been

trained up from the ranks of the Intercolonial, almost every one of these men have disappeared hither by way of dismissal or of retirement under the convenient provisions of the Provident Fund Act, and in some instances illegally retired under the provisions of that Act and disturbing its equilibrium. I could hot speak too strongly with respect to this matter.
Where four years ago on the Intercolonial there were three engineers doing the work, to-day there are fourteen or fifteen men doing the same work. Where did these men come from? In almost every instance they came from the Canadian Pacific railway, where Mr. Gutelius came from. Not only that, but many of them have come there as relatives of Mr. Gutelius, the general manager of the Intercolonial. Intercolonial men displaced, sent out of employment in many instances in mid-winter, deprived of their livelihood! For what purpose? To make room for importations from the Canadian Pacific railway and from the United States.
A few weeks ago I was sitting in court in the county of Westmorland, and I heard the affidavit and application of the chief engineer of the Intercolonial for naturalization. He had been in Canada for some years; he had been in the employment of the Canadian Pacific railway, and his appointment at Moncton was brought about by the displacement of an old and retired Intercolonial engineer, a man against whom naught can be said, a man whose qualifications are the equal if not the superior of those of the importation to whom I refer. Mr. Brown, the chief engineer of the Intercolonial, made application for naturalization. I think it was in December, 1913, but a few weeks ago. At that time he had been in	the employ of
the Intercolonial for nearly a year. Others have not yet made application for naturalization. What is more, some of them were brought from the Canadian Pacific railway; they were pensioners on the Provident Fund of the Canadian Pacific railway, and they are receiving employment from the Government and being paid wages by the Government, while at the same time they are receiving pensions from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Many of these things are the result of this illegal, this improper agreement.

for an action which is disadvantageous to the people of Canada, to the trade of Canada as a whole and to the Intercolonial railway itself. The very discharge of men on the Intercolonial railway and retirement under the Provident Fund provisions disturbs the equilibrium of a great fund provided for the protection of the employees. More than that, it imposes burdens on every young man called into the employ of the Intercolonial railway during this year or in future years. The present administration of the Intercolonial railway is working havoc with its business. The discontinuance of the ' Ocean Limited ' will disturb the traffic between here and the eastern provinces to such an extent that that traffic will not be recovered when the Intercolonial railway begins running the Ocean Limited next spring, if it does begin to run that train. We all know that men get into the habit of going to certain hotels and travelling by certain routes. I believe the Intercolonial railway route is by all odds the best. I am anxious to see the Intercolonial railway succeed in every possible way. But this Government, apparently, seeks to undermine the business of the Intercolonial railway, business that belongs to it properly in view of its location and circumstances. The Government, I say, are chargeable with disturbing that traffic and injuring the Intercolonial railway to that extent.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister made reference to a statement made by Mr. Sutherland, who was acting Minister of Railways in 1903, in respect of freight charges. My right hon. friend knows-and if he does not he should know-that the through traffic over the Intercolonial to St. John and to Halifax is governed by the mileage of the Canadian Pacific railway; that is to say, the shorter mileage of the .competing route governs the freight charges. Although it is upwards of 800 miles over the rails of the Intercolonial between Halifax and Montreal, the freight rates are computed not on that mileage, but on the mileage between Montreal and Halifax by the shortest rail route-that is over the Canadian Pacific railway via the city of St. John. If you take the Intercolonial at Montreal and go to the city of St. John, you travel many more miles, but you pay the same as you pay on the Canadian Pacific railway, which follows a much shorter and more direct route. So that it is the rule of all railway companies to base their charges on the shorter mileage of a competing route;
' therefore the reference that was made by my

right hon. friend does not apply and is no guide in this instance. In brief, tne matter stands this way: This Government, in order to disarrange its mail contract, and void its terms; in order to go behind the ordinary selection that would be made by the steamship companies; in order to render nugatory the binding contracts entered into by them one year ago in respect of mails and transportation, have illegally, improperly and surreptitiously entered into a contract with the Canadian Pacific railway, through a servant of theirs who had no authority whatever to execute such a contract without the approval of the Governor in Council-which latter authority has never been given-and they are seeking to shelter themselves behind that agreement. I wish that this motion were one involving the condemnation of the Department of Railways and Canals and the Government for even permitting to continue an agreement so outrageously wrong and so absolutely without a parallel in the history of railway contracts.

I
do not intend to go into the discussion of the rival claims of St. John and Halifax in this matter. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say that new and first-class terminals, the very best in the world, were to be constructed at St. John and at Halifax in connection with the Intercolonial and with Atlantic transportation from those ports. But there is a view of this matter which has not yet been presented to the House, and for a few moments I intend to ask the attention of hon. gentlemen to that special view. I think I am well in order, inasmuch as the motion calls for a copy of the agreement between the Canadian Pacific and the Intercolonial, and in that agreement is involved the question of transportation charges generally. Four great steamship companies are involved in this discussion and in the motion, and the Government of Canada is to-day dealing with these four great Atlantic transport companies in the matter of the carrying of our mails. But there is also involved in this discussion, as I say, an agreement between the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific. The farmers of the Canadian west are complaining very much of the enormous freight charges upon the wheat and other products of the Canadian west and the most serious charge-and the one to which the attention of this country has been called recently with great vigour-is that of the enormous increase in ocean freight rates that took place within the last two or three years.

We even sent the chairman of our Railway Commission across to the old country to try to find the source of that great increase in ocean freight rates, and the origin of that most serious tax on the wheat and the Hour of the Canadian west. Arrived in the old country, the chairman found that there was a great increase in charges 9 p.m. -I believe he has made a report in the matter. The impression has gained ground in this country that in some way the powers of this Parliament or of the Railway Commission are not sufficient to reach whoever is at the head of this great Atlantic combine which has doubled the rates on ocean freight. To my mind the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in this country is the head of that great ocean combine. The White Star Line, which figures in this contract, is also in that combine, as well as the Canadian Northern's Royal Line, and the Allan Line, which to-day, so far as I can gather, is owned by the Canadian Pacific railway. The only chance I see of reach ing that combine is not by going to England; not by appointing international commissions to investigate the matter, and then going round the world and asking France, [DOT]Germany, Great Britain and the United States to regulate this ocean combine, but the way to reach it is by trying to regulate it in our own country. My view of it- and it has always been my view in this House-is that if we find any corporation in this country which has been created by Parliament and is treating the Canadian public unfairly, then we ought to do business no longer with that company. I contend that before this agreement was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, giving it very substantial advantages in connection with the Intercolonial Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should have been compelled to explain its connection with the combines affecting Atlantic transportation and freights on the Atlantic, and we should have had no further dealings with the Canadian Pacific railway until it declared its willingness to dissolve that pool. The Canadian Pacific railway, the Allan Line, the Royal Line and White Star Line, doing business with the people of Canada to-day, are all in that great combine; they are the people who are doing most unfairly by the farmers of the West. I charge it here that the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway and that company that came here last year, the
Richelieu and Ontario, for the purpose of securing additional legislation, are all in another combine, the details of which will be unfolded in a few days, to control absolutely every boat doing freight business from Duluth right down to the city of Quebec. And all these are being put into another great pool, so that this great combine will control the ocean freight, the river and lake freight, and the railroad freight; in that way one combine will dominate this whole country from the Pacific clean across to the market for our produce, Great Britain. If that is the case, and I challenge any one in this House to deny it, then Parliament should have no dealings with any corporation in the way of giving that corporation increased privileges on our great national railway, without demanding from it an explanation and insisting on that corporation withdrawing from that pool. The Prime Minister this afternoon, in discussing the great port development and the great terminals in connection with the Intercolonial railway at St. John, Quebec, Halifax and Montreal, said that these were to be great ports and great terminals. Are they to be given to the use of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Allan line and the Royal line and the White Star line, while these same companies are in a pool to uphold freight rates to twice what they were two years ago, and who, if allowed to continue this policy, can put the rates up still higher ? Freight rates are the greatest issue in this country. The development of the West turns absolutely on that question. We have had delegations down here asking for free wheat. The movement for free wheat into the United States, to my mind, turns on the question of freight rates more than any other question, and by free wheat competition in freight rates and competition in prices might be secured. And certainly low freight rates will never come if we shut our eyes to the fact that the great railways of this country are the head of the Atlantic pool and that the greatest sinner of all is the Canadian Pacific railway. This same Canadian Pacific railway has been given substantial advantages over the line of the Intercolonial, and I think the time has come to call a halt m this matter and to have no dealings with any corporation that will enter into a combination of that kind. Certainly no more relief, no more legislation of any kind ought to be given to these great corporations without first insisting upon their presenting a clean bill oFTiealth that they are not in that com-

bine, whether on the lakes and rivers or on the ocean. There is no other way to reach them. It was suggested to me to-day that it would be a fine thing to get another great big commission and to send it abroad and to get all the facts about this ocean combine and create international legislation regarding a thing which we can regulate here at home and in this House of Parliament. There is only one way to do it and that is to refuse to have any relations with these railways or to give them any rights and to refuse them any further legislation. I call the attention of the people of the Northwest to the fact that as long as we give them legislation or other substantial relief in the way of money grants or loans or anything, or give them rights over the Intercolonial railway, we will be showing ourselves incapable of taking care of ourselves. We are making them the rulers of this country, we are not making them serve the country as they ought. That is a point that comes home to me in this discussion in regard to transportation questions which demand so much attention in Canada at this moment. While this seems a small agreement and a simple agreement, and it can be terminated, from what I heard to-night, at very short notice, it cannot be terminated too soon for me in view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway is at the head of the ocean combine, and of the further fact that directors of the Canadian Pacific railway are now lining up this great inland navigation deal. I spoke about it here last session when the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company were here for legislation and when they did not get what they wanted, they resorted to other means. It shows that if you take advantage of these men when they come here and insist on them doing what is fair by the Canadian people, you can control these things. I presented the idea to the right hon. leader of the Opposition on several occasions when he was in office that any time these people came as petitioners asking for aid of any kind, asking for legislation and most of all asking for running rights over the Intercolonial railway, they should be denied and should not be listened to in any sense whatever unless they explained their connection with this Atlantic pool, explained their connection with this inland navigation combine and expressed their willingness to withdraw from it. I say it is absurd that a country like Canada cannot control these people, and that the view is going out to the coun-
try now in- all directions that somehow we cannot control them. There is a constitutional cure for every grievance in this country within the walls of our own legislature, within the covers of our own statute book, if we care to use it. When these railways come here as suppliants for money or legislation, for privileges, we must insist, first of all, on asking them to explain their conduct in the past and to explain, as these railways and steamship lines ought to explain, why they are subjecting the Canadian people to this unfair treatment in regard to freight rates. As I said, the question of freight rates is of interest to all Canada. The farmers in the West now are up against it. A commission has been sitting in the West and that commission has found that a farmer can hardly make money out of wheat when he gets 64 cents or 65 cents a bushel, which was the average in Saskatchewan last lear. That commission says it costs over 60 cents to raise wheat. There is no profit in it for the Canadian farmer; if he does not profit 25 cents a bushel on wheat he cannot succeed. This Parliament, if it wishes to protect the rights of the people of this country, must istop making agreements with corporations, and if this agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway can be cancelled in a very short time I say it ought to be cancelled for the simple reason that the Canadian Pacific railway is the head of the Atlantic pool, it is to-day the head of the inland transportation pool, and it controls the freight rates in the West.
What inland transportation pool?

Every inland navigation company on the St. Lawrence and on the lakes, clean up to Duluth or Fort William, or Port Arthur, is being consolidated to-day, and if you read the financial reports from London to-day you will see the first flotation of bonds is being put on the market. If you look at the names connected with it you will see boats called after directors of the Canadian Pacific railway, you will see directors of the Canadian Pacific railway on some other companies that are being consolidated into the combine; and wherever you go you see this enormous combine-and you see it taking the last dollar out of the farmers of the Canadian West. They are committed to what was discarded in the Western States years ago. The principle of the railways in arranging their freight rates in the Western United States some years ago, before the establishment of the Interstate Commerce

Commission, was to take as much out of the farmer for freight rates as would keep him a poor man on the land. That is what we are doing with this vaunted West of ours, we are putting the farmer at the mercy of the transportation companies. We would not even let him have access to the United States market because the competition of the American roads and of the ships going out of the city of New York would perhaps compel a reduction in these freight rates and perhaps the Americans, before we do it, might find a way of breaking up these combines and we might get the benefit in that way. My contention is, and I present it with all respect -to -the House, that it is time we quit talking about these things in the direction of going outside of our own country and getting outside aid to discipline these roads. It is -time to quit dealing with any of these companies that have been proved to be an outlaw in any way, and least of all should we give a road that is an outlaw-and I contend that every company in that steamship combine on the Atlantic is an outlaw-any rights over the property owned by the -people of Canada. To my mind the Intercolonial is the greatest asset Canada has, and it ought to be kept intact, and if we give the Canadian Pacific railway running rights over the Intercolonial why should not we get the same terms from the Canadian Pacific and extend the Intercolonial to Toronto, Winnipeg and British Columbia. I would like to see the Canadian Pacific giving the Intercolonial reciprocal terms over their line!
Sign a similar contract to the one we have now?

Yes, if they will sign it. I would be glad to endorse that if the Intercolonial could go over the Canadian Pacific on equal terms, I am not against all the roads in Canada having running rights over the Intercolonial if they will reciprocate. That would be -a good thing for the Intercolonial; it would get built up in that way. But I do not like a onesided bargain, and I do not like trading with a corporation that to-day is maintaining freight rates away above wh-at they ought to be, and away above the rates that would be imposed upon them if we had some jurisdiction over them. I believe the steamship companies come under our jurisdiction by the powers conferred in the Railway Act, and if that Act does not give us power over these companies we can revise it, so as to reach this ocean combine. But I am against dealing with these corporations at the present time or giving them any privileges over the national property or at the national ports. What good would the Minister of Public Works do this country if he spent $50,000,000 in great terminals at Halifax and St. John and if he allowed the Canadian Pacific to use them and that company charged what it liked on the ocean. We are always doing something new, giving some advantage to somebody, but we are not getting the advantage ourselves -and if we are to have the same experience with the railways as we have had in connection with ocean -freight rates the benefit of our national ports will go to these railways and all they will do is to take advantage of them -and put increased rates on the farmers and business men of the West. That is not good policy. It has got to stop and it must be stopped right away. And that contract, if it can be withdrawn-and I believe it can-ought to be withdrawn in the interests of this country unless the Canadian Pacific can show the Government that they -have a clean record in regard to the Atlantic combine in the matter of freight rates. Otherwise, they should not -have that contract for a day longer than is necessary to cancel it. I have said wh-at I 'have to say -and I think I -have presented this question in a new way. I do not present it in a partisan way at all. I do not want to place any criticism on either side of the House, for wh-at has taken place in the past, but I do want to show this House and all the people of Canada the connection between these railways and these ocean lines and the -high freight rates prevailing in this country. The time has come when there must be no dealing with a transportation company that seeks to control the freight of the railways, to control the cartage agencies even, the lake and river freight and ocean freight, and the farmer who grows the grain and the miller who grinds the flour; and it is_ the western miller who is complaining most bitterly about the Atlantic combine. I say that once for all we ought to stop having dealings with these corporations in the way of giving them running rights and special rates as long as they give the people of Canada most unfair, most unjust and burdensome freight rates in connection with the ocean, in connection with the inland lakes and the railways.

The Postmaster General has not yet told us that he was ignorant of the agreement, and the people of New Brunswick have been greatly impressed with the co-existence of this agreement and the appointment of Mr. Gutelius as General Manager of the Intercolonial railway. Neither the Postmaster General nor the Prime Minister has yet told us whether any legal agreement was made between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway. We know that when the agreement was mooted, the Board of Trade of St. John, composed of citizens of all political parties and of probably more Conservatives than Liberals, appointed a delegation to interview the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways, with regard to that matter, and they were told that so far as these ministers were aware no agreement was in existence. The delegation of the St. John Board of Trade returned to their city in the hope that no such agreement would be brought into force, but almost at the very moment that the delegates were in Ottawa, to protest against the agreement made between Mr. Gutelius for the Intercolonial railway and Mr. Bosworth for the Canadian Pacific railway, Mr. Gutelius was laying it down in the language of a Russian czar to the people of St. John that the agreement would be put in effect. When he was asked if the agreement would be cancelled, the answer he gave to the council of the board of trade was: ' I would not say that, but if you think an agreement signed by the vice-president of one company and by the

general manager of the other is not binding, then you had better go ahead. We know now that Mr. Gutelius put this agreement into operation without even the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. We are told to-day that this agreement is only for six months, but that is long enough for the Intercolonial railway to lose its traffic between St. John and Halifax, and if we did not object to it, there is no doubt that it would possibly be renewed for so long as this Government remains in power.
That will not be long.

I know it will not be long, but in the meantime it is our duty to endeavour to remedy the conditions existing along the line of the Intercolonial railway. As representing a northern New Brunswick constituency, I may say that we have always feared that the construction of other railroads would take away some trade from the Intercolonial railway and reduce that part of it in my district to the position of a local road. That fear has been renewed in our minds by the conduct of this particular official of the Intercolonial railway who has been so severely criticised by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), who was able to speak as an expert. For the information of the Prime Minister and the Postmaster General, who have told us that the agreement was only for six months, I wish to point out that there is an immense discrepancy between the rates charged by the Intercolonial railway to the shippers of the Maritime provinces and the amount charged under this agreement to that wealthy corporation the Canadian Pacific railway, for this traffic between St. John and Halifax, the result of which agreement will be to divert from St. John that traffic which legitimately belongs to it in the winter months.
The freight rates charged by the Intercolonial to the ordinary shippers of freight are ten or fifteen times more than those charged to the Canadian Pacific railway under the Gutelius agreement. The people of the Maritime provinces along the north shore wish this matter rectified just as much as the people of St. John and Halifax do. Here is a comparison of the rates existing at the time of the Gutelius agreement given at the meeting of the St. John Board of Trade.
The freight charges to the general shipper on flour and grain between St. John and Halifax
in carload lots is fourteen cents per hundred' pounds or $2.80 per ton as compared with the Gutelius agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway of three cents per hundred pounds or sixty cents per ton.
The charges to the general shipper on general freight range from thirteen to thirty-five cents' per hundred pounds in carload lots as compared with three and three-fourths cents' per hundred pounds or seventy-five cents per ton under the Gutelius agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway.
General freight charges, so far as the general shipper is concerned, are divided into* ten classes ranging from 35 to 12 cents per hundred pounds. For example the rate for class 1, which includes groceries and glassware, is 35 cents per hundred pounds; the rate for class 5, which includes molasses, sugar etc., is 17 cents per hundred pounds; the rate for class 10, the lowest class, which includes lime, etc., is 13 cents per hundred pounds.
Thus the lowest charge for general freight to the general shipper is 13 cents per hundred pounds, as compared with the rate of 31 cents per hundred pounds under the Gutelius agreement.
The Gutelius agreement states that no train of twelve cars is to exceed in earnings to the Intercolonial railway more than $300. Under ordinary circumstances, a train of twelve cars, carrying 500 people, at $6.25 a piece,-the lowest priced ticket issued between St. John and Halifax, commercial travellers' rates- would exceed in earnings $3,000 for the people's* railway, or, if the train were a freight train of twelve cars, which would be 720 tons, the ordinary rate of $2.80 per ton would mean a revenue to the Intercolonial railway of $2,016, as compared with the $300 under the Gutelius agreement.
Should the cars used be Canadian Pacific railway cars, that would, of course, make some difference in the value of the service.
This shows the difference between the charges which the people of the Maritime provinces are called upon to pay to the Government and the charges to the Canadian Pacific railway under the Gutelius agreement. If it is necessary to impose these charges upon the people of the-Maritime provinces, it is nothing else but robbery to make the people pay for the advantage given to the Canadian Pacific railway. I hope my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) is interested in these figures. They will appear in ' Hansard ' tomorrow for the study of the people of Canada.

What are the facts? The Canadian Pacific railway made up their minds that they were going to bring their large steamers to Halifax this year and to sail them from that port. In order to do so, they had to get running rights over the Intercolonial from St. John to carry the passengers to and from their steamers. I am not one of those who regard it as unfortunate that the Canadian Pacific railway want to run their steamers from Halifax or that the Canadian Pacific railway want to run their trains into Nova Scotia. But when the hon. member for York comes here and wants to dictate what is to be done in regard to the Intercolonial railway, I must tell him that I come from a province where the onlyrailway of any kind which enables us to maintain communication with the rest of the transportation facilities of the country is the Intercolonial railway, and that railway to-day, run with excessive freight rates, without any competition whatever, is a great and onerous charge upon the business interest of that province. ,We want the Canadian Pacific railway, we want the Grand Trunk Pacific when it is completed, and like all the other provinces we have our right to desire every one of these transportation systems within our borders. These systems should not be precluded from going to that province; and, speaking for Nova Scotia, I claim for our people the benefits of competition. When the Canadian Pacific railway decided to come to Nova Scotia, having no railway communication, it was a fair business proposition to go to the Intercolonial railway and ask their permission to came in on fair terms. And when I recall the position taken by the St. John Board of Trade and other gentlemen in regard to this agreement., I recall that there was a lot of talk about what St. John was going to do about it. But why did they not go to the Railway Commission and ask that the agreement be reviewed? I would like to ask the people of St. John, who, as everybody knows, are complaining of the way they are dealt with,. why they did not have that agreement reviewed.

Does the hon.
gentleman contend that it is within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission?

I know it is not, as a matter of fact, but I saw it stated at the time on reliable authority that the Railway Department were willing to submit the terms of this agreement to the Railway Commission, waiving any legal or technical objections.
Would it not be an unfair discrimination, and thereby come within the purview of the Railway Commission?

I am not discussing the technical question whether they could go there or not, because it was understood that they could go there. But what I say is, that the people of St. John should have acted upon their opportunity to go before the Railway Commission and have that agreement reviewed. I was not here when that phase of the subject was under discussion, and do not care now to discuss whether it was too much or too little. Every one in the Maritime provinces knows that the Government in that matter were playing politics. The Canadian Pacific railway wanted to come to Halifax with their big steamers. They decided to come there, no matter what happened. To placate St. John, the influence of the Government and of the Prime Minister, who represents Halifax, was exercised with his particular friends Mackenzie & Mann to take their steamers away from Halifax and send them to St. John. That is the cold English of the situation.
He says no.

If he did not do it
himself, he got somebody else to do it. So far as the facts are concerned, one does not need to have state papers brought down to make clear what any man of ordinary common sense knows to be the fact; as I venture to say that whatever diplomatic denials may be made, it is regarded as a fact.
I am sure the hon. gentleman will accept the word of the Prime Minister.

I am bound to accept his word in this House. It may be that some other member of the Government went and did this thing behind his back. But in the city he represents he is held responsible for the fact that some [DOT]one in his Government arranged the deal 39
under which these two boats of Mackenzie & Mann were taken from the city of Halifax. The idea that they went of their own free will and accord is absurd. Sir William Mackenzie said so. Mr. Hannah kept wiring the people of Halifax day after day up to the eve of the withdrawal of the boats that he was not going to take them away and could not be induced to take them away. That is the situation-the Government is playing off one port against the other. But some day they will have to come out of the woods and settle what they are going to do. Up to that time, I suppose, they can fool the people of St. John and they can fool the people of Halifax.

No, they cannot fool
St. John any more.

They are making a brave effort to do so; and the same with Halifax. That is the whole thing with regard to. this discussion concerning the removal of these steamers. But my purpose in rising is to emphasize the fact that we want the Transcontinental lines in Nova Scotia, and we do not propose to be the only province in the country that is tied up to one railway system. Look at British Columbia. In a few years that province will have every one of our great transcontinental lines in it; and in that province the natural trade flowing to the Pacific through Vancouver does not begin to be as great as that which flows in winter to the Atlantic seaboard. But when we come to the Prime Minister and ask for even necessary railway accommodation, he declines to give it.
Will the hon. gentleman explain to the House how the freight rates have increased now that the Canadian Pacific railway has the right of running over the Intercolonial railway?

The freight rates,
under the Administration of this Government, have increased by leaps and bounds. Within the past year they have increased by almost fifty per cent on staple articles. Representations were made by the business interests of Nova Scotia, and as a result a reduction of this high increase was made, but the average freight increase paid by those interests last year is at least 25 per cent higher. And when we go to the Minister of Railways and ask him to give us merely reasonable railway improvements, we cannot get them. He gives the Prime Minister a road in his own constituency, but he will do nothing for



anybody else. So, I go on record for Nova Scotia as being anxious, for the purpose of competition and increasing of business, to have these transcontinental lines in our province. Under the Liberal Administration, we could send our coal, our iron, our steel, to Montreal in winter at rates that enabled the interests engaged in the production of these articles to make money. To-day, under this Government, through the increased freight rates imposed, it is impossible to send these products, which are staple products in our province, to the centres of industry of Canada. To the question as to what this Government should do in regard to the winter ports, it is time they stopped their shuffling. Every one in the Maritime provinces knows that they have been playing a game, and the sooner they stop it the better.
